title: US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses
detail:
US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses
Lockridge Okoth
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 3:56 PM MST 2 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
^DJI
CL=F
^NDX

Wall Street appeared ready to recover from October's $2 trillion technology stock wipeout on Monday. Within hours, roughly $700 billion in fresh market gains had evaporated.

The S&P 500 surged as much as 1.1% in morning trading before closing down 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1%, extending last week's brutal AI stock selloff.

The reversal came shortly after CNBC host Jim Cramer posted on X:

"Here we go: biggest tech takeout."

He was referring to Marvell's $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum. But the timing quickly revived jokes about Cramer's famously mixed market predictions.

Why Did the Stock Market Rally Suddenly Collapse?

The morning optimism came from the Middle East.

Oil prices dropped to $104 as possible US-Iran peace talks raised hopes of cheaper energy and easing inflation.

Stocks initially jumped. The Nasdaq 100 gained around 1.3%, while the Dow climbed more than 1%.

But investors soon returned to the same concern that erased more than $2 trillion from the Nasdaq 100 during October: How much longer can Big Tech keep spending billions on AI without delivering sufficient returns?

Oracle plunged nearly 9% after announcing plans to raise $20 billion through stock and bond sales to fund its AI expansion. Marvell lost almost 13%.

White House Says AI Has Plenty of Money

Meanwhile, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett dismissed fears of an AI financing crisis.

"There's so much cash in the ecosystem that I think that people should be reassured," Hassett said.

Interestingly, nearly 70% of S&P 500 companies finished higher. The weakness remained concentrated in major technology stocks.

As for Cramer's supposed curse, the Inverse Cramer ETF, designed to bet against his recommendations, lost 15% before closing in 2024.

Investors now face Tuesday's US midterm elections and Friday's jobs report, with confidence in the AI trade already shaken.

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), a specialized cloud computing provider for generative AI workloads, closed at $50.15, down 8.60%. Premarket partnership news with CrowdStrike faded as leverage concerns weighed on the market, and investors are watching Nov. 10 earnings.

Trading volume reached 47.1M shares, coming in nearly 21% above its three-month average of 38.9M shares. CoreWeave IPO'd in 2025 and has grown 25% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) dropped 0.50% to 7,542, and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) fell 1.07% to 25,164. Among peers in AI cloud infrastructure and specialized data center services, Oracle closed at $119.10, down 8.85%, and Nebius Group closed at $141.39, down 8.27%, underscoring weakness across chip-adjacent infrastructure names.

What this means for investors

The latest price action in CoreWeave shows continued shareholder discomfort with the cloud stock's reliance on debt.

Although the expanded partnership with CrowdStrike is objectively good news for the company, the excitement over that deal was short-lived as the stock's downtrend continued.

Customer interest is not the issue. Demand for neocloud infrastructure is insatiable, as CoreWeave's backlog totaled $104 billion, not including Q3 customer commitments.

Still, that demand does the company little good if its ability to finance infrastructure builds remains in question. Considering that industry insiders like Elon Musk think many neoclouds will fail, CoreWeave is likely to remain under the gun for the foreseeable future.

In fairness, CoreWeave is not the only neocloud stock struggling, as both Nebius and Oracle also plunged. However, Oracle still has other legacy businesses, and Nebius is a profitable company with a debt level that's a fraction of CoreWeave's approximate $35 billion in obligations.

The real test for CoreWeave stock may come when it announces its earnings for the third quarter of 2026 on Nov. 10. Factors such as growth, capital expenditures, and debt levels will be where investors will probably focus.

If CoreWeave can continue building infrastructure, address its backlog, and service its debt, it may eventually win back investors' confidence. Nonetheless, any interruptions to this growth could be costly for CoreWeave, making investing in the stock a risky proposition at this time.

title: This Has Been the Best-Performing Stock in the "Magnificent Seven" This Year, and It's Not Even Close
detail:
This Has Been the Best-Performing Stock in the "Magnificent Seven" This Year, and It's Not Even Close
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 2:35 PM MST 4 min read
^GSPC
AAPL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The "Magnificent Seven" stocks are a collection of the leading tech stocks in the world. But this year, they haven't been doing well. The S&P 500 has surprisingly been outperforming nearly all of them. It's particularly surprising given that the broad index is up only 11%. It's doing well, but that doesn't seem like a high bar for stocks to exceed.

Yet, there's only one stock in the Magnificent Seven that has been able to beat it. Ironically, it's the company that has been a bit of a laggard when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI): Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL). Year to date, it's up around 25%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What's behind its rally, and could it go even higher?

Image source: Getty Images.

Apple's cautious spending may be winning over risk-averse investors

While many tech companies are in an aggressive arms race in developing AI chatbots and models as quickly as possible to stay ahead of the competition, Apple's been far more modest by comparison. In fact, customers have become frustrated with its slow pace with respect to AI offerings and its iPhones lagging behind rival phones.

As other stocks in the Magnificent Seven have been spending hundreds of billions of dollars and ramping up spend, Apple modestly forecast $14 billion in capex for its entire fiscal year, unchanged from a year ago. It's perhaps no coincidence then, as investors have become more concerned about high levels of AI spend, that Apple's been the stock of choice among tech investors.

Having a more sensible, calculated, and less aggressive approach to capex has endeared it to the broader market.

AAPL data by YCharts

Is Apple stock still heading higher?

Apple has a terrific business, but the problem is that its stock is now trading at an exceptionally high premium -- close to 40 times its trailing earnings. That's a particular concern for a business that in recent years hasn't often generated more than single-digit growth. There have been times when it's fared better, but also times when it's even performed worse.

Paying such a high premium for fast, high-growth business may be justifiable, but that's not representative of what Apple is. It's a safe, stable tech stock, but it's not what I'd consider to be fast-growing by any means.

Investors who buy the stock at such elevated levels should tread carefully, as it could be vulnerable to a correction in the near future, especially if its upcoming results prove to be underwhelming. Apple is a quality stock to hold for the long haul, but I wouldn't buy it at its current price, as its future returns may be minimal, and at worst, the stock could experience a significant decline given its inflated value.
